A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original node-classification experiments, feature/edge/label deletion analyses, and model-size and reasoning comparisons in Tables 1–5 and Figures 2–4.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds efficiency measurements, summary-prompting experiments, shuffled-adjacency controls and synthetic shortest-path results in Appendices C–D.

M1.justification: Appendix D.1 introduces a summary-prompting variant that recursively summarizes distant neighborhoods before prediction. This changes the prompting procedure, while the original GraphTool, GraphTool+ and Graph-as-Code procedures and templates remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The original 14 node-classification datasets remain. v2 adds synthetic shortest-path regression on Erdős–Rényi graphs, extending evaluation beyond node classification, and introduces shuffled-adjacency test scenarios on seven existing datasets.

E2.justification: Label propagation is added to the homophilic comparisons in Tables 1 and 3, having appeared only in the heterophilic comparison in v1. v2 also adds 2–4-hop summary-prompting comparators and comparisons with GCN, GAT, Encoder GCN, TAPE, LLaGA and UniGraph. The supervised models' scores are explicitly imported from Wu et al. (2025), rather than reported as new runs.

E3.justification: New protocols include token counts and wall-clock latency per query, 2–4-hop summary-prompt evaluation, and shortest-path MSE stratified by path length using 100 graphs of 50 nodes and 100 sampled pairs per graph. Existing dataset splits and deletion-experiment settings are retained; these additions do not establish that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The original deletion heatmaps remain unchanged. v2 adds summarization/hop-depth sensitivity analysis, an adjacency-shuffling control investigating structural dependence versus code-generation priors, token/latency analyses, and a concrete Graph-as-Code execution-log case study.

E5.justification: Existing five-run averaging and ± reporting are retained. Appendix D.2 newly specifies averaging over 10 independent adjacency permutations for the shuffled-graph experiment; this is a new experiment's repetition scheme, not an increase in the earlier experiments' run counts.

E6.justification: Shared entries in Tables 1–5 and the original heatmaps retain their values. Substantial new results appear in Tables 6–11 and the added label-propagation rows, including cora label-propagation accuracy of 76.61±1.94, photo 2-hop summary-prompt accuracy of 86.00, and reported zero shortest-path MSE for Graph-as-Code. These are added results, not improvements to previously reported scores.

T1.justification: The graph and node-classification definitions in Section 3 and label-propagation equations in Section 4 are unchanged. Neither version contains theoretical proofs, and the new experiments introduce no substantive theoretical derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory findings and conclusion retain the same central claims: Graph-as-Code performs strongest overall, particularly on long-text or high-degree graphs; LLM interaction modes remain effective under heterophily; and code generation adaptively uses structure, features and labels.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations involving information loss from recursive summarization, structural dependence versus code-generation priors, deterministic BFS execution, and dataset-driven latency. Appendix D.4 also acknowledges that supervised hybrid LLM–GNN models generally outperform LLM-only methods and discusses their complementary architectural strengths.

D1.justification: v2 newly identifies the default o4-mini context window as 200,000 tokens and supplies procedural descriptions for the added experiments and a concrete pandas execution trace. Existing interaction templates, hardware information and dataset splits are retained. The new reproducibility statement largely points to already documented material.

R1.justification: A new hybrid LLM–GNN discussion adds LLaGA, LangTopo, TAPE and UniGraph references and distinguishes trained hybrid systems from the study's frozen-LLM inference setting. The earlier coding-capabilities discussion moves from Section 2 to Appendix A without substantive revision.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative remain intact. v2 relocates coding-related work, reorganizes the original appendices as B, F and G, adds ethics and reproducibility statements, and makes limited wording and heading edits.

P2.justification: v2 adopts the ICLR layout with changed margins, headings and display scaling, adds six substantive tables and a boxed execution example, and expands Tables 1 and 3. Figures 1–4 retain identical image content but are resized or repositioned. The original dataset-statistics table becomes Table 12.

improvement.justification: Additional baselines, structural controls, efficiency measurements and supervised-model context strengthen the study while preserving its original evidence. However, new reporting errors limit the gain: Table 10 gives an overall prompting MSE of 2.82 although every path-length subgroup is at most 2.29, and D.1's claim of consistently improved summary prompting contradicts Table 8 on reddit and instagram. The additions support a limited net improvement, with weakened confidence in some new interpretations.
